items.excerpt: 15 November 2026• Update: 15 November 2026 Here's a rundown of all the news you need to know for Sunday, including US air traffic control system stable after a nationwide outage, according to the US aviation officials; Iran's Revolutionary Guard saying 2 oil tankers hit mines and caught fire near the Strait of Hormuz; and the Kremlin saying Putin, Xi and Trump will hold a trilateral meeting in southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Nov. 19. The US air traffic control system remained stable following a nationwide outage, but thousands of flights were expected to be canceled as airlines worked to restore normal operations, said Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Administrator Bryan Bedford. "This morning, the system remains stable, and our airline partners are working through the operational recovery," Bedford told reporters at a news conference with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. Bedford said airlines were expected to cancel between 4,000 and 5,000 of the approximately 41,000 flights scheduled as they worked to reposition aircraft and crews stranded by the nationwide ground stop. - 2 oil tankers hit mines, catch fire near Strait of Hormuz: Iran's Revolutionary Guard Two oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire south of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said. The force said the vessels were attempting to pass through the waterway undetected along an unauthorized route, with their navigation and automatic identification systems switched off. The Iranian naval force said the mine strikes triggered explosions and large fires aboard the tankers. - Kremlin says Putin, Xi, Trump to hold trilateral meeting in Shenzhen on Nov. 19 A trilateral meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump will be held Nov. 19 in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. In an interview with Russian state news agency Tass, Peskov said, “An agreement has been reached to hold a trilateral meeting on the 19th between President Putin, Chairman Xi and President Trump. This meeting will take place in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit.” The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit is scheduled for Nov. 18 - 19 in Shenzhen.

The order was lifted late Friday, and federal authorities predicted a full recovery by late Sunday. He warns this could allow Russia to weaken NATO and reshape borders. On Friday, Zelenskyy said Moscow might use these talks to change European security rather than focus on ending the war. He also said that the U.S. asked if Ukraine would withdraw from parts of Donbas in exchange for NATO membership. Zelenskyy insists Ukraine won't surrender territory. He stresses any security changes in Europe must be decided by European NATO members after the war ends.

items.title: US Fed keen on the need to increase policy rates | The Manila Times
items.excerpt: November 15, 2026 SAN FRANCISCO Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said on Friday that her "bias" is that the central bank will need to increase its policy rate, particularly with services inflation moving in the wrong direction and some signs of inflation persistence. "We're going to need to, in all likelihood, raise rates; I will deliberate this with my colleagues in December at our meeting and in all future meetings and make the collective decision that we judge is most appropriate for the economy that is evolving," Daly said at a University of Nevada, Las Vegas Center for Business and Economic Research forecast event. "Producers are telling us more and more that they're running out of room to take it out of margins, and they really want to consider passing along this to consumers. So that's the inflationary impulse we want to avoid." The core consumer price index, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, has risen about 0.3 percent month over month in each of the last three months. That's far higher than the 0.2 percent or less that would be consistent with year-over-year inflation at 2 percent, the Fed's target. Daly, like several other policymakers, said she's particularly concerned that services inflation excluding housing is "not moving in the correct direction," which is particularly troubling because that slice of inflation tends to be sticky. "That's a place where you might think a retailer, or a professional business, if they have to buy more expensive IT goods, pay higher energy bills and have other inputs that are rising in price, maybe they're going to pass that along to customers," she said. The Fed raised its policy rate in September but held it steady in October, and financial markets are betting heavily on quarter-point interest-rate hikes at each of the Fed's December 8-9 and January 26-27 meetings. Daly said she feels markets understand how the Fed sets rates in response to economic conditions, without remarking specifically on the timing of coming rate hikes. Daly said she is also paying close attention to consumer spending, which accounts for most of the US economy, as the December meeting approaches. "Consumer spending remains just surprisingly resilient; you just haven't seen a pullback, so I think that's the piece of information that I'm really looking for in the next one to two to three months: what happens in that, especially around the holiday season, do we see consumers giving up or do we see them keeping going even if prices rise?" Daly said. "Sitting here in Las Vegas...we're just starting to hear that the consumer may be running out of gas. And we're hearing that now in other states, not just Nevada."

items.title: Inflation will be key to future interest rate decisions: US Fed official
items.excerpt: San Diego [US], November 15: US Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip N Jefferson has said that inflation will be the key factor in determining future interest rate decisions, as price pressures remain elevated despite signs of stability in the American economy and labour market. Speaking at the University of California, San Diego Economic Roundtable on Friday, Jefferson said, "Accordingly, I see the trajectory of inflation as providing the more important signal for determining the appropriate stance of monetary policy." He added, "Going forward, I believe that further policy adjustments should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks." Jefferson's remarks come as US inflation continues to remain well above the Federal Reserve's 2 per cent target. According to the data cited in his speech, the annual personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation rate stood at 3.6 per cent in September, while core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, was 3.1 per cent. Expressing concern over persistent price pressures, Jefferson said, "I remain concerned about the risk of higher energy prices leading to a persistent rise in inflation more broadly." He noted that higher energy costs were affecting sectors such as airfares and transportation, while strong demand for new technologies was also pushing up prices of certain goods, including memory chips. Jefferson said inflation data received so far for October remained consistent with price pressures staying well above the Fed's target. On the labour market, he said conditions had stabilised, with the unemployment rate standing at 4.1 per cent in October. "I expect the unemployment rate to stay around its current level in the near term-a level I view as consistent with maximum employment," he said. Jefferson also noted that the US economy had gained momentum this year, with gross domestic product (GDP) expanding at an annualised rate of 3.4 per cent in the third quarter. "The economy has gained momentum this year, expanding at a pace roughly in line with its potential," he said.

items.title: US consumer prices increase strongly for third straight month - Business Recorder
items.excerpt: By Reuters WASHINGTON: US consumer prices increased more than expected in October, driven by higher costs for food and accommodation, leaving the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates next month. The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department on Tuesday also showed a strong buildup of underlying inflation pressures for the third straight month. The Labor Department’s Bureau of Labour Statistics did not publish year-over-year inflation readings because last year’s federal government shutdown prevented the collection of consumer price data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base. Annual consumer inflation jumped 3.7 percent in September. Inflation is running well above the US central bank’s 2 percent target. The US-Israeli war with Iran has boosted oil prices, combining with the import tariffs implemented by the Trump administration last year to lift the cost of living. High inflation contributed to the heavy losses suffered by President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections last week. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday that the US central bank should raise rates next month, adding that “a stronger policy move may be needed.” Waller also raised the prospect of a 50 basis point hike if core consumer prices, excluding food and energy, increased 0.3 percent or more from September, which they did. “Consumers’ inflation nightmare continues with no relief in sight,” said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. “Fed officials are going to need to bring a bigger hose if they have any hope of putting the inflation fire out.” The CPI increased 0.4 percent last month after advancing 0.6 percent in September. It was the third consecutive month of CPI gains of 0.4 percent or more. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI climbing 0.3 percent over the month. Shelter, which includes rents, hotel and motel rooms, accounted for more than 30 percent of the increase in the CPI last month. Shelter costs rose 0.3 percent after climbing 0.4 percent in September. Food prices surged 0.5 percent after barely rising in the prior three months. Grocery store prices rebounded 0.4 percent, boosted by a 0.9 percent jump in the cost of beef. Egg prices rose 0.6 percent while fruits and vegetables were 0.6 percent more expensive. Prices for dairy and related products rose 0.6 percent. The cost of snacks surged 1.0 percent. Higher prices at the supermarket could be a reflection of more expensive diesel fuel. The cost of eating out also increased last month, with prices of food away from home surging 0.5 percent after rising 0.2 percent in September. The cost of full service meals increased 0.7 percent. Gasoline prices climbed 1.0 percent after soaring 9.1 percent. Though diesel prices have come down from record highs, they rose 2.7 percent last month after increasing 11.9 percent in September. STRONG CORE INFLATION Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI increased 0.3 percent in October, advancing by the same margin for three months in a row. The so-called core CPI was forecast to have climbed 0.2 percent in October. Core CPI inflation increased 2.6 percent year-over-year in September. It was last month driven by a 0.3 percent rise in owners’ equivalent rent, a measure of the amount homeowners would pay to rent or would earn from renting their property. Prices for hotel and motel rooms rose 0.6 percent. Airline fares rose 0.4 percent. The cost of recreation increased 0.8 percent, while motor vehicle insurance advanced 0.7 percent. Household furnishings and supplies prices rebounded 0.7 percent, suggesting that some pass-through from tariffs remained.

items.excerpt: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers. The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would “irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest." The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that “We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons.” He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild ”a World Championship Public Facility." Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. “They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it,” she wrote. “Both points favor granting Plaintiffs’ motion for another temporary restraining order.” With shifting Iran rhetoric following US elections, Trump leaves Mideast in limbo about path ahead WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has had a lot to say about his thinking on the way ahead in the Iran war since Republicans were trounced in last week's midterm elections. In exchanges with reporters, broadcast interviews and social media posts since Election Day, he's somehow managed to back away from carrying out additional strikes while also backing away from the prospect of additional talks with the Islamic Republic's negotiators on ending the 8-month-old conflict. The president acknowledged on the day after the midterms that the war and the global economic tumult it's caused were partly to blame for Republicans' electoral losses, while maintaining it was the right thing to do. Then, at the start of this week, he huddled with Qatar's prime minister at the White House and afterward told reporters that he believed it was highly unlikely he'd need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over.” But by Thursday, he was again raising questions about whether he needed to rush to find an endgame. He declared that the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Tehran and brusquely directed Vice President JD Vance — who served as his chief negotiator in earlier peace talks with Iran — to shift his attention to the administration's domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democrat-controlled cities and states.

Glenn Close and Ridley Scott to get honorary Oscars at Governors Awards LOS ANGELES (AP) — Glenn Close will finally hold an Oscar and make an acceptance speech after eight nominations without a win. She will receive an honorary Academy Award for her five-decade career at the Governors Awards on Sunday night. Director Ridley Scott of films like “Alien” and “Gladiator” will also receive an honorary Oscar. He plans to accept via recorded video. Disney animator Floyd Norman and producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler will be honored too. Close shares the record with Peter O’Toole for the most nominations without a win. She has won other major awards throughout her long career, including Emmys, Golden Globes and Tonys. LOS ANGELES (AP) — Phil Collins gave an emotional acceptance speech at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony. He received a tribute from Cynthia Erivo and was inducted Saturday night by Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker. Collins, who uses canes due to health issues, was honored for his dual stardom as a drummer and pop singer. Oprah Winfrey inducted the late Luther Vandross, praising his impact on love songs. U2 surprised the audience by opening the show with their new single. MC Lyte and Sade were also inducted, with hip-hop acts like Wu-Tang Clan and Queen Latifah making their presence known at the event in Los Angeles. LOS ANGELES (AP) — The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame has inducted its 2026 class of 18 musical legends at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. Artists become eligible 25 years after their first release. Luther Vandross, known for his velvet-voiced love songs, was inducted by Oprah Winfrey. Usher performed a medley of his hits. MC Lyte, a trailblazing rapper, received the Early Influence Award. Sade was inducted by Andra Day, with a performance of “Smooth Operator.” Ed Sullivan was honored for his influence on rock and roll. Other inductees include Phil Collins, Billy Idol, Wu-Tang Clan, and Queen Latifah. Richard Sterban, the bass vocalist of the Grammy-award winning gospel quartet The Oak Ridge Boys and a country music hall of famer, has died. He was 83. His family and the band say he died Saturday in Hendersonville, Tennessee, due to complications from bronchitis and pneumonia after a long battle with cancer. Sterban was a native of New Jersey. He left his job as a backup singer for Elvis Presley to join the vocal group, best known perhaps for its rendition of “Elvira.” The band won five Grammy awards, and its members were inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015. In 2011 they gained membership in the Grand Ole Opry. Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler, co-founders of Killer Films, are making history Sunday with their honorary Oscar at the Governors Awards. They are the first female producing team and independent producers to receive the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award. Known for bold, independent films like “Boys Don’t Cry” and “Safe,” they have produced over 100 films. Their work has been pivotal in New Queer Cinema and includes cult classics like “Hedwig and the Angry Inch.” Despite challenges, they remain optimistic and continue to create innovative films. They have a new project, “De Noche,” starring Pedro Pascal and Danny Ramirez. Bobby Pulido is a member-elect for the U.S. House of Representatives who has also recently won the Latin Grammy for best Tejano album. He accepted the award Thursday at a ceremony in Las Vegas that reflected a broader trend of political advocacy in music. Pulido recently won a competitive race to flip Texas’ 15th Congressional District. He announced his retirement from music onstage and other artists called for unity and representation. Daddy Yankee and Anitta highlighted issues in Puerto Rico and Brazil. Political references had long been dormant from the awards. ... BANGKOK (AP) — Filipino singer Carmelle won the first Asian edition of the Eurovision Song Contest with a fiery performance of “Sobra-Sobra,” beating 10 other acts in the grand final in Bangkok. Votes from national juries and viewers worldwide determined the winner. Thai duo Mang x Daou placed second with “Aroma,” followed by Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên with “Em Tiên.” Contestants arrived on tuk-tuks, waving their national flags. Bulgarian singer Dara, winner of the 70th Eurovision Song Contest, performed as a special guest. The contest seeks to put music first, though it often faces political challenges.
